claim: Male little torrent frogs possess a rich repertoire of visual displays involving the movements of limbs.
source: Male little torrent frogs possess a rich repertoire of visual displays involving the movements of limbs.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Results section describing the diversity of limb displays observed in the study species.

claim: Toe trembling (TT) involves vibrating, wiggling, or twitching the toes, with the arm and leg motionless.
source: Toe trembling (TT): Vibrating, wiggling, or twitching the toes, with the arm and leg motionless (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1A.

claim: Hind foot lifting (HFL) involves raising one hind foot towards the dorsal direction and then returning it back on the ground, without extending the leg.
source: Hind foot lifting (HFL): Raising one hind foot towards the dorsal direction and then returning it back on the ground, without extending the leg (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1B.

claim: Arm waving (AW) involves lifting one of two arms and waving it up and down in an arc toward the front of head.
source: Arm waving (AW): Lifting one of two arms and waving it up and down in an arc toward the front of head (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1C.

claim: Limb shaking (LSA) involves rapid movements of hand or foot in an up-and-down pattern.
source: Limb shaking (LSA): Rapid movements of hand or foot in an up-and-down pattern (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1D.

claim: Wiping (W) involves moving a hand or foot on the ground, with the limb not fully extended.
source: Wiping (W): Moving a hand or foot on the ground, with the limb not fully extended (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1E.

claim: Leg stretching (LS) involves stretching one leg or both legs at the substrate level.
source: Leg stretching (LS): Stretching one leg or both legs at the substrate level (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1F.

claim: Foot flagging (FF) involves raising one or both legs off the substrate level, extending it/them out and back in an arc shape, and then getting it/them back to the ground.
source: Foot flagging (FF): Raising one or both legs off the substrate level, extending it/them out and back in an arc shape, and then getting it/them back to the ground (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a descriptive definition of a specific limb movement type, supported by visual documentation in Figure 1G.

claim: Calling males produce more defensive arm waving (AW) displays than silent males (W=895, p<0.001).

evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing calling and silent males, presented in Figure 4.

source: We found calling males to produce more defensive AW (Wilcoxon rank sum test; W=895; p<0.001), W (W=872.5; p<0.001), LSA (W=755; p=0.032) and HFL (W=736.5; p=0.053) display than silent males (Figure 4), presumably because calling individuals attracted more parasites than silent individuals.

claim: Females expressed a strong preference to approach a male that performed an arm waving (AW) movement compared to a motionless male (probability = 0.81, N=16, p=0.021).
source: Females expressed a strong preference during audio-visual playbacks to approach a male that performed an AW (probability = 0.81; N=16; p=0.021; Figure 5A) or HFL (probability = 0.76; N=21; p=0.027; Figure 5B) movement when compared to a motionless male (static control).
evidence: This is a result from female mate choice experiments, presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Females expressed a strong preference to approach a male that performed a hind foot lifting (HFL) movement compared to a motionless male (probability = 0.76, N=21, p=0.027).
source: Females expressed a strong preference during audio-visual playbacks to approach a male that performed an AW (probability = 0.81; N=16; p=0.021; Figure 5A) or HFL (probability = 0.76; N=21; p=0.027; Figure 5B) movement when compared to a motionless male (static control).
evidence: This is a result from female mate choice experiments, presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Females did not express a preference for the wiping (W) display during audio-visual stimulus presentation (probability = 0.48, N=31, p=1).
source: Females did not express a preference for the W display (probability = 0.48; N=31; p=1; Figure 5C) and the LSA display (probability = 0.57; N=28; p=0.572; Figure 5D) during audio-visual stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a result from female mate choice experiments, presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Females did not express a preference for the limb shaking (LSA) display during audio-visual stimulus presentation (probability = 0.57, N=28, p=0.572).

claim: Females did not express a preference for the AW/HFL stimuli versus motionless stimuli in the absence of an advertisement call (probability = 0.47, N=19, p=1).

claim: The attractive movements (AW and HFL) were strongly associated with advertisement calls.

claim: The two movements (AW and HFL) were followed by calls with a probability of 62%.
source: The two movements were followed by calls with a probability of 62%, while calls only were followed with movements in 39% of cases.

claim: Males use more exaggerated displays (LS + FF) when females are nearby.
source: These data suggest that males use more exaggerated displays (i.e. LS + FF) when females are nearby.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from field observations of male-female interactions.

claim: A higher proportion of males produce LS and FF displays when females are nearby compared to when females are not around (N1=4, N2=39, p=0.001).
source: We found a higher proportion of males to produce LS and FF displays (the most exaggerated limb movements in little torrent frogs) when females were nearby (Fisher's exact test; N1=4, N2=39; p=0.001; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing male behavior in the presence versus absence of females, presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Only 5 out of 39 recorded males emitted LS + FF movements when females or other males were not around.
source: Only 5 out of 39 recorded males emitted LS + FF movements when females or other males were not around (i.e. long-range signaling), while all recorded individuals had such movements when females appeared nearby (i.e. close-range signaling).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from field recordings comparing long-range and close-range signaling contexts.

claim: All recorded individuals had LS + FF movements when females appeared nearby.
source: Only 5 out of 39 recorded males emitted LS + FF movements when females or other males were not around (i.e. long-range signaling), while all recorded individuals had such movements when females appeared nearby (i.e. close-range signaling).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from field recordings of male-female interactions.

claim: Males produced more exaggerated displays (LS + FF) when females were in close range compared to long-range distance (N1=4, N2=39, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, males produced more of those exaggerated displays when females were in close range compared to long-range distance (Wilcoxon rank sum test; N1=4, N2=39; p<0.001; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing the frequency of exaggerated displays at different distances, presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Several limb displays (AW, HFL, and LS + FF) can serve as visual signal components and influence female mate choice.
source: By performing female choice tests and observing male-female interactions in the field, we showed that several of these limb displays (AW, HFL, and LS + FF) can serve as visual signal components and influence female mate choice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results and field observations.

claim: All limb movements could be spontaneously generated, but their rates were increased by call-induced parasite presence.

claim: Females showed a strong preference for males that emitted advertisement calls accompanied by parasite-evoked movements (e.g. AW and HFL).
source: Such parasite-host interactions may have important evolutionary consequences because females in our choice tests showed a strong preference for males that emitted advertisement calls accompanied by parasite-evoked movements (e.g. AW and HFL).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mate choice experiments.

claim: Females did not show preference for limb movements in the absence of call playback.
source: We did not find such preference for limb movements in the absence of call playback, demonstrating that these visual components are part of a multimodal display.
evidence: This is a result from the mate choice experiments testing visual stimuli without acoustic signals.

claim: The visual components (limb movements) are part of a multimodal display.
source: We did not find such preference for limb movements in the absence of call playback, demonstrating that these visual components are part of a multimodal display.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that limb movements only influence female preference when combined with acoustic signals.

claim: Multimodal signaling can be highly complex, often involving multiple underlying neuronal motor programs that need to be synchronized in order to perform well.
source: Such multimodal signaling can be highly complex, often involving multiple underlying neuronal motor programs that need to be synchronized in order to perform well (Partan and Marler, 1999; Ryan et al., 2019; Halfwerk et al., 2019; Higham and Hebets, 2013).
evidence: This is a general statement about multimodal signaling supported by multiple citations.

claim: The production and reception of multimodal signals is often more costly in terms of energy loss or predation and parasitism risk when compared to unimodal signals.
source: The production and reception of multimodal signals is often more costly in terms of energy loss or predation and parasitism risk when compared to unimodal signals (Bro-Jørgensen, 2010), and their evolution is therefore often explained through functional benefits, such as cross-modal perception by receivers, which can improve signal detection and discrimination, or enhance attention and memory time (Halfwerk et al., 2019; Hebets and Papaj, 2004; Halfwerk et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is a general statement about multimodal signaling costs supported by a citation.
